subtopic_detail: deciding what must be excluded before iron is replaced in a middle aged man with microcytic anaemia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old man who has become breathless walking up the hill to his house over the past three months. He puts it down to getting older and having given up cycling.

He has no abdominal pain, has not noticed any blood in his stool and says his bowels are unchanged. He takes no aspirin, no anti-inflammatory medication and no anticoagulant. He drinks four standard drinks a week and has never had a gastroscopy or colonoscopy. He has not been invited to bowel screening because he moved address. His father had a colectomy in his sixties for a reason he was never told. His weight is stable and he has no night sweats. His examination shows conjunctival pallor with no abdominal mass, no organomegaly and a normal rectal examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 86/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no koilonychia, abdomen soft with no mass or organomegaly, rectal examination normal with brown stool
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 72 fL (80-100), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 6 percent (16-45), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral iron and recheck the full blood count after three months of therapy
options.rationale: Iron replacement is certainly needed and will correct the haemoglobin, and giving it without investigating the cause allows a colonic malignancy to progress while the blood count normalises and falsely reassures both of you. Replacement and investigation proceed together rather than one instead of the other. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy and colonoscopy while commencing iron replacement
options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man or a postmenopausal woman is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation because a right sided colonic carcinoma can bleed occultly for months without altering bowel habit or producing visible blood. His family history of colectomy in his sixties raises that risk further, and iron is started at the same time rather than afterwards. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Request a faecal occult blood test and investigate further only if it is positive
options.rationale: Faecal occult blood testing is a population screening tool for asymptomatic people, and using it in someone who already has established iron deficiency anaemia adds nothing, because the anaemia is itself the evidence of blood loss. A negative result would not exclude a tumour and would delay endoscopy. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Perform haemoglobin electrophoresis before any endoscopic investigation is arranged
options.rationale: Electrophoresis distinguishes thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency in an unexplained microcytosis, and that question is already answered here by a ferritin of 7 micrograms/L with a transferrin saturation of 6 percent. Thalassaemia trait also does not deplete iron stores. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron infusion and review his symptoms again in six weeks
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is appropriate where oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, or where rapid correction is needed, and the route of replacement is not the issue in this case. Whichever route is chosen, the underlying source of loss still has to be found. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in an adult man or a postmenopausal woman is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and the absence of visible bleeding or altered bowel habit is expected rather than reassuring. Right sided colonic tumours characteristically present exactly this way, with occult blood loss and anaemia rather than obstruction, because the caecum is capacious and the stool is liquid there. Bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation, because upper and lower tract lesions are both common and synchronous pathology occurs. Coeliac serology should be checked, as here, since coeliac disease is a treatable non bleeding cause. Iron replacement is started at the same time as referral, never instead of it.
key_points: Iron deficiency anaemia in men and postmenopausal women mandates investigation of the gastrointestinal tract.
Right sided colonic tumours bleed occultly without altering bowel habit or producing visible blood.
Bidirectional endoscopy is required because upper and lower lesions are both common and may coexist.
Faecal occult blood testing adds nothing once iron deficiency anaemia is established.
Coeliac serology should be checked as a treatable non bleeding cause of iron deficiency.
explanation.pearls: Never accept a normal rectal examination and a normal bowel habit as a reason to skip colonoscopy in a man with iron deficiency anaemia, because a caecal carcinoma bleeds into liquid stool in a capacious lumen and typically declares itself only as breathlessness and a low ferritin.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia
Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

subtopic_detail: completing assessment of a discrete breast lump when the imaging report is reassuring but the clinical findings are not
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47 year old woman who found a lump in her left breast three weeks ago while showering. She has no breast pain and no nipple discharge.

She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and has never taken hormonal contraception. She had a screening mammogram eighteen months ago that was reported as normal. On examination there is a 2 cm firm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast that does not move freely within the breast tissue, and there is mild tethering of the overlying skin when she raises her arm. There is no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Bilateral mammography and targeted ultrasound arranged by a colleague last week are both reported as showing no discrete abnormality in dense breast tissue.

data_table.Examination: 2 cm firm irregular mass in the left upper outer quadrant with reduced mobility and skin tethering on arm elevation, no nipple retraction or discharge, no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, right breast normal
data_table.Investigations: Bilateral mammography reports heterogeneously dense breast tissue with no discrete abnormality, targeted left breast ultrasound reports no discrete lesion identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for core biopsy of the palpable abnormality despite the imaging result
options.rationale: Triple assessment requires clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling to be concordant, and when any one component is suspicious the assessment is incomplete until tissue has been obtained regardless of how reassuring the others are. Mammographic sensitivity falls substantially in dense breast tissue and some cancers, particularly invasive lobular carcinoma, infiltrate diffusely without forming a discrete sonographic mass, so a negative scan cannot override a tethered irregular lump. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Reassure her that both imaging tests are normal and review her in three months
options.rationale: Interval review is appropriate for a clinically benign finding such as a soft mobile lump in a younger woman with concordant normal imaging. Discordance between a suspicious examination and negative imaging is the specific situation in which reassurance is unsafe, and three months allows nodal progression. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Repeat the mammogram with tomosynthesis views in a further six months time
options.rationale: Tomosynthesis does improve cancer detection in dense tissue and would be a sensible adjunct at the time of assessment rather than a reason to wait half a year. Repeating imaging also cannot substitute for the histology that a palpable suspicious mass requires. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Arrange fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass in the practice this week
options.rationale: Fine needle aspiration can confirm malignancy but cannot distinguish invasive carcinoma from ductal carcinoma in situ, and it does not provide receptor status or grade, which now guide neoadjuvant decisions. Core biopsy has superseded it as the sampling method for a solid breast mass. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Check her serum tumour markers and refer only if the results are abnormal
options.rationale: Serum markers such as CA15-3 have no role in the diagnosis of breast cancer because they lack both sensitivity and specificity in early disease, and they are used only for monitoring established metastatic disease. A normal result would wrongly reassure everyone involved. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

explanation.summary: Triple assessment of a breast lump comprises clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling, and its central principle is concordance: if any component raises suspicion, the workup continues until that suspicion is resolved by histology. This woman has a firm irregular tethered mass, which is a clinically suspicious finding regardless of what the imaging shows. Mammographic sensitivity is substantially reduced in heterogeneously dense breast tissue, and invasive lobular carcinoma characteristically infiltrates in single file without forming a discrete mass on either mammography or ultrasound. A normal screening mammogram eighteen months earlier does not exclude an interval cancer. Core biopsy rather than fine needle aspiration is the sampling method, because it distinguishes invasive from in situ disease and provides grade and receptor status.
key_points: Triple assessment requires concordance, and any suspicious component mandates tissue sampling.
Mammographic sensitivity is substantially reduced in dense breast tissue.
Invasive lobular carcinoma may infiltrate without forming a discrete mass on mammography or ultrasound.
Core biopsy is preferred over fine needle aspiration because it provides grade, invasion status and receptor status.
Serum tumour markers have no role in diagnosing early breast cancer.
explanation.pearls: Refer a clinically suspicious breast lump for core biopsy even when mammography and ultrasound are both reported as normal, because discordance is resolved by histology and invasive lobular carcinoma in dense tissue is the classic cancer that both imaging modalities miss.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

subtopic_detail: separating an arrhythmic cause of collapse from a benign faint using the history and electrocardiogram
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 34 year old man who collapsed while playing indoor soccer an hour ago. His teammates say he dropped without warning, was briefly stiff with a few jerks, and was fully alert within thirty seconds.

He had no warmth, nausea, tunnel vision or sweating beforehand, and he does not remember falling. He has had two similar episodes in the past year, one while sprinting for a bus and one while swimming, both of which he attributed to dehydration. He has no tongue biting, no incontinence and no confusion afterwards. His father died suddenly at 41 while jogging and was never autopsied. He takes no medication and uses no drugs. He is currently asymptomatic with normal observations, and his examination reveals a systolic murmur that becomes louder when he stands up from squatting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg lying and 122/74 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on standing from squatting and on Valsalva, jerky carotid upstroke, no ankle oedema, chest clear, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in the lateral leads, electrolytes and troponin within normal limits, capillary glucose 5.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with advice on hydration and salt intake for a vasovagal tendency
options.rationale: Reflex syncope is common and is managed this way, and it is identified by a prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating or visual greying, by an upright provoking situation such as prolonged standing or venepuncture, and by a normal heart and electrocardiogram. Syncope occurring during exertion without any prodrome is the opposite pattern and is never attributed to a reflex cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Arrange outpatient tilt table testing to confirm a neurally mediated mechanism
options.rationale: Tilt testing is used for recurrent unexplained syncope where a reflex mechanism is suspected and the cardiac workup is clean. Using it in a man with exertional syncope, a family history of sudden death and an abnormal electrocardiogram risks a falsely reassuring positive result while he remains at risk of sudden death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Load with an antiepileptic and refer to neurology for outpatient investigation
options.rationale: Brief stiffening with a few jerks is common in syncope of any cause once cerebral perfusion falls, and it is not evidence of epilepsy. A genuine seizure is suggested by tongue biting, incontinence and postictal confusion lasting minutes, and he recovered fully within thirty seconds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Admit for continuous cardiac monitoring with urgent inpatient echocardiography
options.rationale: Syncope during exertion with no prodrome, a family history of sudden death under 50, a murmur that increases with reduced preload and an electrocardiogram showing hypertrophy with lateral T wave inversion together identify a structural cardiac cause with a real risk of ventricular arrhythmia. Admission with telemetry protects him while echocardiography defines the outflow tract and wall thickness, and this pathway also captures the family screening that a heritable cardiomyopathy requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Fit a 24 hour ambulatory monitor and review him in the clinic next week
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring is reasonable for infrequent palpitations or for syncope judged to be low risk, and a 24 hour recording is very unlikely to capture an event that has occurred three times in a year. Sending him home while awaiting the result leaves him unmonitored during the interval in which he is most at risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Most syncope is reflex and benign, so the clinical task is to identify the minority in whom it signals a risk of sudden death. The high risk features present here are syncope occurring during exertion rather than after it, complete absence of a prodrome, recurrence, and a family history of sudden death under 50 years. Examination adds a murmur that becomes louder on standing from squatting and on Valsalva, which indicates dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction because reduced preload worsens it, in contrast to aortic stenosis where the murmur softens. The electrocardiogram showing left ventricular hypertrophy with deep lateral T wave inversion supports hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Brief myoclonic jerking during syncope is common and does not indicate epilepsy, and these patients need admission, telemetry and echocardiography rather than outpatient investigation.
key_points: Syncope during exertion, without prodrome, or with a family history of sudden death is high risk.
A murmur that increases with reduced preload indicates dynamic outflow obstruction rather than valvular stenosis.
Left ventricular hypertrophy with deep lateral T wave inversion suggests hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Brief stiffening and jerking occur commonly in syncope and do not indicate a seizure.
Tongue biting, incontinence and prolonged postictal confusion distinguish a genuine seizure from syncope.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the collapse happened during exertion or after it, because syncope during exertion points to a structural or arrhythmic cause needing admission, whereas syncope immediately after stopping exercise is usually reflex and benign.

subtopic_detail: managing a small solid pulmonary nodule found incidentally in a former smoker with no prior imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64 year old woman after a computed tomography scan of the abdomen performed for suspected renal colic, which incidentally captured the lung bases and reported a 7 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe with smooth margins.

She smoked fifteen cigarettes a day from age eighteen until she stopped nine years ago. She has no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain and no weight loss, and her exercise tolerance is unchanged. She has never had a chest radiograph or chest computed tomography before, so there is no earlier imaging for comparison. She has no history of malignancy and no known asbestos exposure. Her examination is normal with no lymphadenopathy, no clubbing and a clear chest. The radiologist notes no mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no pleural abnormality.

data_table.Examination: No clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation with equal expansion, no chest wall tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography reports a 7 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe with smooth margins, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy, no pleural effusion, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for computed tomography guided percutaneous biopsy of the nodule
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy is used for larger or more suspicious peripheral lesions where a tissue diagnosis will direct treatment, and at 7 mm the target is small enough that the non diagnostic rate is high while the pneumothorax risk is unchanged. Sampling is not justified before surveillance has shown whether the nodule is growing. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Arrange positron emission tomography to characterise the metabolic activity
options.rationale: Functional imaging is valuable for nodules above about 8 to 10 mm, and below that size its spatial resolution produces frequent false negatives because partial volume effects understate uptake. A negative scan at 7 mm would provide false reassurance rather than information. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Refer for bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound and transbronchial sampling
options.rationale: Bronchoscopic sampling is suited to central lesions and to mediastinal nodal staging, and the yield for a small peripheral nodule without a bronchus leading to it is poor. There is also no nodal disease here to stage. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Reassure her that a nodule of this size in a former smoker requires no follow up
options.rationale: Discharge without follow up is appropriate for a nodule below about 5 mm in a low risk person, or for one with benign features such as dense central or laminated calcification or macroscopic fat. A 7 mm solid nodule in a former smoker with a substantial history sits above the threshold at which surveillance is recommended. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Interval computed tomography surveillance determined by nodule diameter
options.rationale: A solid nodule of this size carries a low but not negligible malignancy risk, and growth over time is the most useful discriminator available, so serial thin section computed tomography at intervals set by size and risk is the accepted approach. Surveillance continues for around two years because stability of a solid nodule over that period effectively excludes malignancy, whereas any interval growth prompts escalation to functional imaging or sampling. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

explanation.summary: Incidental pulmonary nodules are found frequently as computed tomography use increases, and management is determined by nodule size, attenuation, morphology and the patient's risk of lung cancer. Comparison with any earlier imaging is the single most valuable first step because documented stability over two years effectively excludes malignancy in a solid nodule, and here no earlier imaging exists. For a solid nodule of this size in a person with a smoking history, interval computed tomography surveillance is recommended, with the interval determined by diameter and risk. Positron emission tomography is unreliable below about 8 to 10 mm because of partial volume effects, and biopsy of a 7 mm target has a high non diagnostic rate. Subsolid and part solid nodules follow different and longer surveillance schedules because indolent adenocarcinoma can grow very slowly.
key_points: Nodule size, attenuation, margin morphology and smoking history together determine management.
Documented stability of a solid nodule over two years effectively excludes malignancy.
Positron emission tomography is unreliable below about 8 to 10 mm because of partial volume effects.
Spiculated margins, upper lobe location and larger size increase the probability of malignancy.
Subsolid and part solid nodules require longer surveillance because indolent adenocarcinoma grows slowly.
explanation.pearls: Hunt for any previous chest imaging before arranging surveillance for an incidental nodule, because two years of documented stability on an old scan resolves a solid nodule immediately and spares the patient a further two years of interval computed tomography.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: preventing acute urate nephropathy before treating a bulky haematological malignancy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34 year old man with a three week history of rapidly enlarging cervical and abdominal lymphadenopathy and night sweats. Biopsy has confirmed a high grade B cell lymphoma with a very high proliferation index, and chemotherapy is planned to start tomorrow.

He has a large abdominal nodal mass and hepatosplenomegaly. He has no history of gout and takes no regular medication. He is of Southern European background and his glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase level has been requested but has not yet returned. He is passing urine normally. His lactate dehydrogenase is markedly raised, his urate is elevated, his potassium and phosphate are at the upper end of normal and his corrected calcium is at the lower end. His creatinine is mildly raised and his urine output has been adequate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bulky cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, abdominal mass palpable in the left upper quadrant, liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, no oedema, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate dehydrogenase 1 840 U/L (120-250), urate 0.58 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), potassium 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 1.48 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), corrected calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before chemotherapy begins?

options.text: Oral allopurinol with encouragement to increase his oral fluid intake
options.rationale: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and so prevents the formation of new urate, which makes it appropriate prophylaxis for low and intermediate risk disease. It cannot remove the urate that has already accumulated, and oral fluids are inadequate for a patient whose urate is already raised with a rising creatinine. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Prophylactic haemodialysis via a temporary catheter before the first cycle
options.rationale: Dialysis is used for established tumour lysis syndrome with refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload or oliguric renal failure. Inserting a line and dialysing prophylactically exposes him to procedural risk when pharmacological prevention has not yet been tried. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine and improve urate clearance
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation was standard practice and has been abandoned because raising the urinary pH increases the deposition of calcium phosphate in the renal tubules, worsening nephrocalcinosis in a patient who is already hyperphosphataemic. It also exacerbates the hypocalcaemia. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Delay chemotherapy for one week and repeat the biochemistry before proceeding
options.rationale: Delay would be reasonable for a slow growing tumour requiring optimisation, and a high grade lymphoma with this proliferation index can double in days, so waiting increases both the tumour burden and the eventual lysis risk. The metabolic risk is managed alongside treatment rather than by postponing it. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous hydration with rasburicase once the enzyme result has returned
options.rationale: Bulky rapidly proliferating disease with a markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase, an elevated urate and impaired renal function places him at high risk, and rasburicase converts existing urate to the far more soluble allantoin rather than merely preventing further production. Vigorous intravenous hydration to maintain high urine output is given alongside, and confirming glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status first matters because rasburicase causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficient patients. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when rapid cell death releases intracellular contents, producing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and consequent hypocalcaemia, with acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate deposition in the tubules. Risk is determined by tumour bulk, proliferation rate, baseline lactate dehydrogenase and urate, and pre-existing renal impairment, and this man is high risk on every count. Allopurinol prevents new urate formation and suits lower risk patients, whereas rasburicase enzymatically degrades urate already present and is indicated for high risk disease. Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status must be established first because rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and causes severe haemolysis in deficient individuals, who are more commonly of Mediterranean, African or South East Asian ancestry. Urinary alkalinisation has been abandoned because it promotes calcium phosphate precipitation, and vigorous hydration with close biochemical monitoring remains the foundation of prevention.
key_points: The metabolic signature is hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hypocalcaemia.
Allopurinol prevents new urate formation while rasburicase degrades urate already present.
Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is a contraindication to rasburicase because of severe haemolysis.
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium phosphate deposition.
Vigorous intravenous hydration with frequent biochemical monitoring is the foundation of prevention.
explanation.pearls: Check glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status before giving rasburicase, because the drug generates hydrogen peroxide and causes life threatening haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficient patients, who are disproportionately of Mediterranean, African or South East Asian ancestry.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand
